context: The torn bush at the end of Canto 13 held the soul of a Florentine suicide, who begged to have his leaves gathered. Dante does it for the sake of the city they share.

note: Dante's Italian says ring, not circle. This is the line between the second and third rings of the seventh circle: the wood of the suicides ends and the burning sand begins.

quote: rejects every plant from its bed
note: The third ring is barren sand. It holds those violent against God, and against nature and human work, which Dante counts as God's child and grandchild (Canto 11). They turned on the source of life, and nothing grows here.
The river of boiling blood of Canto 12. The three rings are nested: the river circles the wood, and the wood circles the sand.

context: During the civil war against Caesar he marched the remains of the republican army across the Libyan desert. The Roman poet Lucan describes the march, with its heat and serpents, in his epic on the civil war.

note: Three groups, three postures. Those lying face up are the blasphemers, violent against God. Those sitting are the usurers (Canto 17). Those forever walking are the sodomites (Cantos 15–16). The blasphemers are fewest and suffer most, taking the fire full on.
The fire and brimstone that God rained on Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis 19. It falls slowly and silently, like snow, which makes it worse.

context: The story comes from a letter Alexander was supposed to have written to Aristotle about the marvels of India. Dante seems to follow a retelling by the scholar Albert the Great, which runs together a heavy snowfall the soldiers trampled and a later rain of fire.

note: Tinder under the flint and steel used to strike a fire. The sand catches and burns, so the souls are scorched from below as well as from above.
Dante's word is tresca, a quick country dance with much slapping of hands. The souls beat at themselves without rest to brush the fire off.
The gate of the city of Dis, where the fallen angels slammed the door in Virgil's face and only a messenger from Heaven could open it (Inferno 8–9). It is the one time Virgil's authority has failed.

quote: What I was living, I am dead!
note: He boasts that death and damnation have not changed him. That is exactly his punishment: the souls in Hell are fixed forever as what they chose to be.

context: Capaneus keeps up his quarrel with the god who killed him, daring him to throw every thunderbolt he has.

note: Vulcan, the smith of the gods, who forges Jupiter's thunderbolts. "The others" are his helpers, the one-eyed Cyclopes, and their workshop was said to lie under Mount Etna, the volcano in Sicily.
The plain where the giants, sons of Earth, tried to storm the home of the gods and were struck down by Jupiter's lightning. Dante meets the giants themselves in Inferno 31.

context: A pagan who cursed a pagan god stands for the sin of blasphemy. What matters to Dante is the attitude: a creature's raging contempt for the power above it.

quote: No torment except your own rage
note: The fire is not the worst of it. His fury can never be satisfied and never stop, and so it torments him more than anything laid on him from outside.

The Seven against Thebes. When Oedipus's son Eteocles refused to give up the throne to his brother Polynices, Polynices brought seven champions and their armies against the city. Dante knew the story from the Thebaid of Statius.

quote: the perfect ornament for his chest
note: Sarcasm. The decoration his proud chest has earned is his own spite.

context: An overflow of the river of blood. It runs out of the wood and straight across the sand toward the center, in a stone channel.

note: A hot sulfur spring near Viterbo, north of Rome, well known in Dante's day as a bathing place. Its steaming water was led off in channels.

Usually taken as the prostitutes of the place, who had the spring water piped to their own houses because they were barred from the public baths. A few scholars read a different word here, meaning women who worked hemp in the water.

quote: whose threshold is denied to none
note: The outer gate of Hell, with the inscription of Canto 3. It stands open to everyone, always.

quote: quenches all the flames above it
note: The steam rising from the stream puts out the falling fire. Its stone banks are therefore the only safe path across the sand, and the poets will walk on them through the next two cantos.
Virgil has made Dante hungry to know why this little stream is so remarkable. Dante asks him to feed the appetite he has raised.
The island lies near the middle of the Mediterranean, between Europe, Asia and Africa, the three parts of the world Dante knew. The Aeneid calls it the cradle of the Trojan race, and so of Rome.
Saturn, father of Jupiter. In Roman myth his reign was the Golden Age, when people lived in peace and innocence, without laws or labor.
The highest mountain of Crete. In the myth it was green and full of springs. Dante makes it a dead place, like the age of innocence it once sheltered.

Saturn's wife. Saturn had been warned that a son would overthrow him, and swallowed each of his children at birth. Rhea hid the baby Jupiter on Ida, and had her priests shout and clash their weapons to drown out his crying.

context: The statue is the human race through history. Its back is to the East, where the old empires rose, and it looks toward Rome, the seat of empire and Church, where history is now being decided.

note: The metals grow baser from the head down, like the ages of the world: gold, silver, brass, iron. The image comes from the statue King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of in the Book of Daniel (chapter 2), and from the four ages in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

quote: the right foot is baked clay
note: The meaning is disputed. The most common reading takes the two feet as the two powers meant to guide mankind: the iron foot is the Empire, and the clay foot is the Church, weakened by wealth and worldly power, yet the one on which the world now leans most.

Every age since the golden one is broken by sin, and what flows from the break is human sorrow. The tears of all history drain down into Hell and become its rivers. The suffering of the damned is made of the evil done on earth.

The four rivers are one stream under four names. It is the Acheron at the edge of Hell, the swamp of Styx in the fifth circle, the Phlegethon of boiling blood here in the seventh, and at the bottom it freezes into Cocytus.

quote: where there is no more descending
note: The center of the earth, the lowest point in Dante's universe. From there every direction is up.

The poets go down through Hell in a spiral, bearing left at each level. They cross only a part of each circle, so they have not yet gone once around, and there are things on every level they never pass.

context: Dante knows from the Aeneid that Lethe is a river of the underworld, and wonders why Virgil left it out. Virgil answers that it is not in Hell at all.

note: The rain of tears from the statue, not the rain of fire. Dante has not understood that he has already seen Phlegethon.
Phlegethon means flaming in Greek, and the Aeneid describes it as a river of fire. Virgil thinks the boiling river of blood should have told Dante which river it was.

quote: where souls go to wash themselves
note: The top of Mount Purgatory. Souls who have finished their penance drink from Lethe there and lose the memory of their sins. Dante drinks from it himself in Purgatorio 31.
